14-039.r: Largest FDI inflow in 2007-08 (and over the last decade) → services sector.

14-041.r: Largest FDI share in 1997-2000 → services sector; in the last 3 years (2021-2024) Computer Software and Hardware led, then services.

14-042.r: India attracted large foreign investment in life insurance, banking and automobiles; services (incl. banking, insurance) got 16.13% of FDI, April 2000 to March 2024.

14-043.r: Foreign exchange earning opportunities in India → tourism, medical care, garments and leather goods: all four.

14-044.r: FDI equity inflow April-September 2022 → Karnataka highest among options (5329 million USD); Maharashtra highest overall (8000 million USD).

14-045.r: Bihar, April-June 2018 → service sector attracted the highest FDI equity inflow.

14-046.r: Largest foreign exchange inflow to India in 2005-06 (among options) → portfolio investment.

14-047.r: Most volatile foreign exchange flows → NRI deposits and foreign portfolio investment; they chase interest rate gaps and leave when rates turn unfavourable.

14-048.r: Hot currency (hot money) → foreign currency that moves quickly between markets chasing the highest short-term interest rates.

14-049.r: Tight US Fed policy can cause capital flight; capital flight can raise interest cost of firms with ECBs; devaluation increases (not decreases) ECB currency risk.

14-050.r: Tobin Tax (after economist James Tobin) → tax on foreign exchange (spot currency conversion) transactions to curb short-term currency speculation.

14-051.r: FDI → largely non-debt creating capital flow; investment in an unlisted Indian company, or ten percent or more of a listed company's equity.

14-052.r: FDI includes subsidiaries of foreign companies, majority foreign equity in Indian firms and firms fully financed by foreign companies; portfolio investment is not FDI.

14-053.r: Counted as FDI → FCCBs, foreign institutional investment with conditions, GDRs/ADRs; non-resident external deposits are debt-creating inflows, not FDI.

14-054.r: FCNR(A) → 1975, RBI bore exchange rate risk, withdrawn 1993; FCNR(B) from 15 May 1993, banks bear the risk; only scheme A withdrawn.

14-055.r: Lesson of East Asian and Latin American crises → FDI is the best inflow (stable); excess volatile portfolio investment caused the crises.

14-056.r: FDI vs FII: FII raises capital availability in general (short-term, secondary market); FDI targets specific sectors, is more stable, brings technology and management.

14-057.r: Buying bonds or stocks of an overseas pharma company → portfolio investment, not FDI; acquiring a mill, a wholly owned firm or a new plant abroad are FDI.

14-058.r: Participatory Notes (P-Notes) → issued by registered FIIs to overseas investors who invest in Indian stocks without registering with SEBI (started 2000).

14-059.r: Participatory Note → issued by SEBI-registered foreign portfolio investors to overseas investors wanting Indian stocks without direct registration (overseas derivative instrument).

14-060.r: Union Budget 2020-21 → FPI limit in outstanding corporate bonds raised from 9% to 15%.

14-061.r: Largest FDI equity source: Mauritius in the question period and cumulative; Singapore in recent years (US$ 11,774 million in 2023-24), then Mauritius, USA.
14-061.c: Printed answer (b) Singapore uses recent data; the explanation says Mauritius (d) was correct for the question period.

14-063.r: Largest FDI sources to India in 1991-95 → USA and Japan.

14-064.r: Top FDI equity sources in 2016-17 → Mauritius > Singapore > Japan; in 2023-24 → Singapore > Mauritius > USA > Netherlands > Japan.

14-065.r: Large FDI from Mauritius → India's Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) with Mauritius; investors route capital via Mauritius to pay less tax.

14-066.r: Economic Survey 2022-23: FDI fell in the first half of FY23 due to weak global economy, though still above pre-pandemic levels; only statement 4.

14-067.r: FATCA (US law, 2010) → India-US IGA signed 9 July 2015, operational from 30 September 2015; shares offshore account information against tax evasion.

14-068.r: FDI 2001-02: tea sector foreign firm to disinvest 26% (not 33%) within 5 years; print media foreign capital max 26%, largest Indian shareholder above 26%.

14-069.r: Calendar year 2005 → foreign institutional investors invested about US$ 10.7 billion in Indian companies.

14-070.r: FIPB moved to Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance in January 2003; abolished in 2017 (approvals now by administrative ministries).
14-070.c: Options are misprinted (two '(b)' labels); the answer (d) stands for Ministry of Finance.

14-071.r: FDI opened in retail trade: single-brand 51% (2006), multi-brand 51% (2012); 100% single-brand with 30% local sourcing.

14-072.r: Foreign-owned e-commerce: 100% FDI only in marketplace model; cannot sell own inventory; vendor deemed controlled if over 25% of its purchases come from the marketplace.

14-073.r: FDI in insurance: proposal on 4 October 2012 to raise it from 26% to 49%; Budget 2021-22 raised it from 49% to 74% (effective 19 May 2021).

14-075.r: Foreign equity in small scale units, 1995-96 → up to 24%; above 24% of paid-up capital the unit lost its SSI status.

14-076.r: Debt trap → a country must take new loans just to pay interest on old loans.

14-077.r: India's external debt crossed US$ 300 billion by end-2010; US$ 624.7 billion at end-March 2023; US$ 648.2 billion at end-December 2023.

14-078.r: India's external debt is mostly non-government (US$ 506.0 billion of US$ 648.2 billion, end-December 2023) and not all in US dollars: both statements false.

14-079.r: Major component of India's external debt → commercial borrowings (about 38% in 2017; 33.2% at end-December 2023).

14-080.r: India's external debt rose from US$ 98,158 million (March 2000) to US$ 100,225 million (March 2001) due to commercial borrowings and NRI deposits.

14-081.r: External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs) → regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (eligible borrowers, end use, maturity, all-in-cost ceiling).

14-082.r: World Bank Global Development Finance 2010 → most indebted: Russia, China, Turkey, Brazil, India; end-December 2022: China, Brazil, India, Mexico, Turkey.

14-083.r: Largest external debt → USA (US$ 24.5 trillion, 26.3% of global debt, end-December 2022), then UK, France, Germany, Japan.

14-084.r: World Bank classifies India as a less indebted country; external debt-to-GDP 18.7% at end-December 2023.

14-085.r: Largest World Bank borrower after India (till June 2010) → Mexico; in 2022 India had the highest IBRD/IDA debt stock (US$ 38.26 billion).

14-086.r: May 2001 → India gave Tajikistan a US$ 5 million grant to tackle drought.

14-087.r: October 2001 → Germany granted a US$ 32 million credit for the Tehri dam project (Uttarakhand).

14-088.r: Green bonds → fixed-income, low-cost loans with long (not short) maturities for climate projects; first issued by European Investment Bank in 2007; World Bank in 2008.
14-088.t: The first green bond came from the European Investment Bank ('Climate Awareness Bond'), not a 'Fund' as option (b) says.

14-089.r: India Millennium Deposit scheme → launched 21 October 2000 by SBI for NRIs (not residents); five-year deposits at 8.5%; raised $ 5.5 billion.

14-090.r: Resurgent India Bonds (SBI, 5 August 1998) → issued in US dollar, Pound Sterling and Deutsche Mark for five years.
14-090.t: Don't confuse: Resurgent India Bonds → Deutsche Mark; India Millennium Deposits → euro.

14-091.r: Masala Bonds → rupee-denominated bonds issued abroad by Indian entities, so the issuer is shielded from currency risk; fund infrastructure and internationalise the rupee.

14-092.r: IFC (World Bank arm) issued the first Masala bond in November 2014; rupee-denominated debt for public and private sector; RBI allowed corporates on 29 September 2015.

14-093.r: Oil-Pool Account closed with abolition of the Administered Price Mechanism (APM) in oil on 1-4-2002 (Finance Minister Yashwant Sinha).

14-094.r: Import cover → number of months of imports a country's international reserves can pay for; 11 months at end-December 2023.

14-095.r: India's forex reserves, 2018-19 (end-March 2019) → Rs. 28,55,882 crore; 29 March 2024 → Rs. 53,84,281 crore (US$ 645.58 billion).

14-096.r: RBI: forex reserves in 2018-19 (end-March 2019) → US$ 412871 million; on 29 March 2024 → US$ 645.58 billion.

14-097.r: India's forex reserves (held by RBI) → foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and reserve tranche position in IMF; so 'SDRs not included' is false.

14-098.r: Largest share in India's forex reserves → foreign currency assets (US$ 570618 million on 29 March 2024), then gold, SDRs, IMF reserve position.

14-099.r: India's forex reserves → foreign currency assets, RBI gold, SDRs and IMF reserve tranche; loans from World Bank or foreign countries are not included.
14-099.h: FGSR: Foreign currency, Gold, SDRs, Reserve tranche.

14-101.r: Forex reserves were US$ 129.7 billion on 10 December 2004 (above 125 billion); WPI series from April 2000 had base 1993-94; current base 2011-12.

14-102.r: NEER rise → rupee appreciation; REER rise → loss (not gain) of trade competitiveness; higher domestic inflation than abroad widens the NEER–REER gap.

14-103.r: A currency's price in the international market → set by demand for the country's goods/services and its government's stability; the World Bank has no role.
